## ARTICLE INFO --- *Article history:* Received 8 May 2021 Revised 10 June 2021 Accepted 16 June 2021 Available online 18 June 2021 --- *Keywords:* Anthracene Deep eutectic solvents Separation mechanism Intermolecular interaction

ABSTRACT Anthracene (AN) is an important fine chemical feedstock, mainly derived from the anthracene oil fraction of high-temperature coal tar. The traditional solvent crystallization method used to obtain anthracene involves large amounts of solvents. A method with a high separation capacity and a high selectivity needs to be developed urgently. To this end, the composition of crude AN oil and the solubility of its main components in xylene were determined, and phenanthrene in crude AN oil was extracted with xylene. Pure deep eutectic solvents (DESs) and DESs–organic solvent mixture were then applied to separate anthracene and carbazole, respectively. Based on the distribution coefficient, selectivity, and purity of the AN product, the influence of organic solvent type, the molar ratio of DESs to organic solvent, and DESs type on the separation efficiency were investigated. Finally, the separation mechanism was investigated with density functional theory calculations and UV-visible spectroscopy. The results show that the phenanthrene content decreased from 25.5% to 2.6% and most of other condensed aromatics in crude AN were removed after washing twice with xylene. DESs–organic solvent mixtures had better performance than pure DESs for the separation of anthracene and carbazole, and under optimal condition, the 97.5% purity of AN is acquired in a single separation step with a tetraethyl ammonium chloride–glycerol DESs–DMF mixture. The more complicated interactions between phenanthrene and xylene than between anthracene / carbazole and xylene favored the removal of phenanthrene. The hydrogen bond with the minimum bond energy (–17.6 kJ/mol) between DESs and carbazole is also stronger than that with the maximum bond energy (–16.8 kJ/mol) between DESs and anthracene. Adding DESs to organic solvent can enhance the interactions between carbazole and the solvent, but had no significantly influence on interactions between anthracene and the solvent, thereby facilitating the separation of anthracene and carbazole. © 2021 Elsevier B.V. ## 1. Introduction Crude anthracene oil, a fraction distilled from high-temperature coal tar, is a mixture consisting of condensed aromatic compounds with 2–5 aromatic rings [1]. Among the condensed aromatics are anthracene (AN), carbazole (CAR), and phenanthrene (PHE), which account for more than 1 wt% of high-temperature coal tar. AN, one of the most valuable components in coal tar, is an irreplaceable raw material in the manufacture of dyes, bactericides, pesticides, light-emitting diodes, and so on [2,3]. For the production of fine chemicals, AN with a purity higher than 98% is essential. The remaining 2% impurities, which are difficult to remove, include CAR [4]. Much effort is need to improve the purity of AN while refining crude AN

Commonly used methods to isolate AN include distillation, supercritical fluid extraction, zone melting, emulsion membrane separation, and solvent crystallization [5-7] and each method has its own advantages and disadvantages [7,8]. For example, distillation has the advantage of continuous operation and the disadvantage of high energy consumption; supercritical fluids extraction has a high extraction efficiency for aromatics, but require harsh operating conditions; the zone melting technique is complex to operate, and the emulsion membrane separation method is unstable. Ionic liquids (ILs), known as green solvents, are also being investigated in the refining of crude AN oil, and it was shown that 66.6% recovery and 90.2% purity of CAR separated from anthracene oil could be achieved [9]. However, as a new separation technology, the use of ILs in crude AN oil refining still faces difficulties in implementation [10], requiring further investigations and studies.

Solvent crystallization is a common but efficient separation and purification method because it is a low energy consumption and easy process. Unfortunately, repeated crystallization processes consume large amounts of solvent. Due to the similarity in structure of AN and CAR, solvent extraction processes cannot guarantee large distribution coefficients and high selectivity. In recent studies, the AN purity attained by solvent extraction typically reached 90–95% [11], with a maximum purity of about 97% [12]. Due to the limitations of these separation techniques, a new method using a third component in traditional organic solvents was proposed and yielded promising results. For instance, adding supercritical CO2 to acetone promoted the separation of AN and PHE [13]; dissolving an amide/amine combination in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) improved the solubility of PHE in that solvent [11]. In research by Ye et al. [7,14], it was shown that the addition of isopropanolamine, urea, and H2O to DMF improved the separation selectivity for AN and CAR significantly. The enhanced separation efficiency was ascribed to the electron-rich atoms or groups in the additives, introducing intermolecular interactions such as hydrogen bonds with the –NH group of CAR [14]. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), similar to ILs, have a broad liquid temperature range, a low vapor pressure, a high chemical stability, and were used for the removal of CAR from fuels [15]. Due to the formation of hydrogen bond between the DESs and CAR, efficient fuel denitrogenation was achieved. DESs include both hydrogen bond donors and hydrogen bond acceptors, facilitating the formation of intermolecular interactions with target components. Correspondingly, the performance of DESs was excellent in the extraction and isolation of many components including phenolic compounds [16,17], nitrogen/sulfur- containing compounds [18], benzene derivatives [19], and metals [20]. The application of DESs as solvents or additives to refine crude AN oil has not been reported, however.

In this study, the solubility of AN, PHE, and CAR in xylene were determined and PHE was first extracted from crude AN oil with xylene. DESs were then used as separation agents or additives in organic solvent for the separation of AN and CAR. The separation efficiency of DESs, either pure or mixed with solvents was investi- gated, as well as the separation mechanism involved.

## 2. Experimental and calculation section ### 2.1. Chemical reagents Analytical pure Anthracene (AN), carbazole (CAR), and phenanthrene (PHE) were purchased from Macleans Reagent Co., Ltd. Glycerol (99 wt%), levulinic acid (99 wt%), malonic acid (99.5 wt%), 9-fluorenone (98 wt%), Tetraethyl ammonium chloride (TEAC, 98 wt%), and tetrapropylammonium chloride (TPAC, 98 wt%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co. Analytical pure N,N-dimethyl formamide (DMF), N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP), N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA), hexane, and xylene were purchased from Tianjin Kemiou Chemical Co. Acetonitrile (HPLC pure) was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co.
Crude anthracene oil was provided by one steel factory, Wuhan, China. The composition was detected by GC-MS (7890B GC system, 5977A MSD; Agilent Technology).

## 2.2. Preparation of DESs and AN-CAR mixture The preparation procedure for TEAC–glycerol DESs was provided herein as an example, where TEAC and glycerol were selected as the HBA and HBD, respectively. In a typical process, TEAC and glycerol were mixed at equimolar ratio in a capped conical flask and agitated with magnetic stirring at 80 °C until the liquid became homogeneous. Other DESs were prepared in a similar way.
AN-CAR mixture was prepared by dissolving AN and CAR in hot benzene and evaporating benzene after AN and CAR were completely dissolved.

2.3. Separation experiments Separation of AN and CAR. The AN–CAR mixture was added to the prepared DESs and stirred magnetically for 30 min at the set temperature. Filtered them to obtain cake and filtrate at room temperature. A small amount of cake and filtrate were respectively collected and analyzed by the UV–visible spectrophotometer. The

Separation of crude anthracene oil. The crude anthracene oil mainly contains 34.1 wt% AN, 25.5 wt% PHE, and 16.4 wt% CAR. The separation experiment on crude anthracene oil was conducted as follows: 100 g crude anthracene oil and 60 ml xylene were mixed in a 500 ml flask equipped with a reflux condenser pipe and stirred magnetically for 30 min at 120 °C in an oil bath. After the crude anthracene oil was completely dissolved in xylene, this mixture was filtered at 30 °C to obtain the first filter cake. Subse- quently, the first filter cake was mixed with xylene at the liquid/- solid ratio of 1.5:1 and the conditions of stirring and filtering were the same as the above. And the second filter cake rich in AN and CAR was obtained and dried at 40 °C for 12 h. The dried second fil- ter cake was mixed with DESS-DMF solvent, magnetically stirred at a set temperature for 30 min, and filtered at room temperature to get AN product. Take a small amount of product for GC detection to determine the purity.

## 2.4. Analytical methods The content of AN and CAR in cake and filtrate for measuring distribution coefficient was analyzed by UV-visible spectrophotometer (CARY 300). The UV-vis absorption peaks of CAR and AN at 292 nm and 378 nm had no overlap and no mutual interference (Figure S1 of supporting information) and they were selected as the characteristic absorption wavelengths of CAR and AN respectively for quantitative calculation. UV-visible spectral experiments were also carried out to verify the interactions between solvent and AN or CAR. The sample scan range was 220 to 420 nm.

The compositions of crude AN oil and AN product were detected by GC–MS (7890B GC system, 5977A MSD; Agilent Technology), equipped with a HP-5 capillary column (30 m × 0.32 mm × 0.25 µm) and a flame ionization detector (FID). The chromatographic detection temperature conditions were 280 °C for the over and injector, and 300 °C for the detector. The MS detection conditions were a temperature of 250 °C for the detector, 70 eV emission volt- age, and mass range of 33–400 Da.

2.5. DFT calculations DFT calculations were performed using G09 program package [21]. More than five initial geometries for compound or conformation were optimized under no symmetry restrictions at the M06-2X/6-31 + G(d,p) level. The frequency was analyzed at the M06-2X/6-31 + G(d,p) level and lack of imaginary frequencies for the optimized structures indicated minimum energy structures. The single-point energy was computed at the M06-2X/6-311++G (d,p) level and the counterpoise procedure [22] was considered to correct the basis set superposition error (BSSE). The interaction energy, ΔE, was computed using equation (3):
ΔΕ = Ε(Α... Β) - E(A) – E(B) + BSSE (3)
Localized orbital locator (LOL) [23] integrated π over plane (LOLIPOP) and LOL-π map were used to measure and analyze π- stacking ability and aromaticity of AN, PHE and CAR. Electrostatic

potential (ESP) [24] was used to analyze nucleophilic and elec- trophilic sites of AN, PHE and CAR. Reduced density gradient (RDG) [25] was used to analyze the weak interaction between xylene and AN or PHE or CAR. Independent gradient model (IGM) [26] was used to visually study the interactions between DESS and AN, CAR, or DMF. Atoms in molecules (AIM) population [27] was used to identify the hydrogen bond and van der Waals (vdW) interaction. The wave function was analyzed using the pro- gram Multiwfn 3.6 [28] and all the isosurfaces were described using VMD 1.9.2 [29].

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Removal of PHE from crude AN oil The composition of crude AN oil is shown in Fig. 1. PHE (25.5%), AN (34.1%), and CAR (16.4%) were the main components of crude AN oil, with small amounts of fluorene, dibenzofuran, dibenzothio-phene and other fused ring aromatic compounds. Note that 9-fluorenone was used as internal standard for the analysis. Xylene, an aromatic solvent, was used to extract PHE from the crude AN oil. Before the separation, the solubility of AN, PHE, and CAR in xylene and the solubility selectivity for PHE vs. CAR (AN) were determined as described in the Supporting Information (SI); the result obtained summarized in Fig. 2. It can be seen that at 30 °C, the solubility of PHE in xylene was nearly 38 times higher than CAR and 18 times higher than AN, indicating that xylene is capable of removing PHE from crude AN oil. Similarly to PHE, xylene is a weakly polar molecule, so it can dissolve a certain amount of PHE in agreement with the "like dissolves like" rule. The dipole moments calculated (at m062x/def2-TZVPD level) for AN, CAR, PHE and xylene were 0, 1.66, 0.01, and 0.42 D, respectively. AN is a non-polar molecule due to its completely symmetrical structure, while CAR is strongly polar due to its -NH bond. Clearly, the inter-actions between xylene and AN or CAR are insufficient to compete with the interactions between AN molecules or CAR molecules, resulting in low solubility of AN and CAR in xylene. At increased temperatures, the solubility of PHE, AN, and CAR in xylene increased to different extents, but the solubility selectivity (SS) for PHE vs. CAR (AN)decreased. To ensure the efficient removal of PHE, the crystal filtration temperature was therefore set to 30 °C. The PHE was removed best by washing twice with xylene, because for a constant total amount of solvent, the operation efficiency is higher according to the "small quantity, many times" rule [30]. The GC analysis results for crude AN oil after the removal of PHE are shown in Figure S2 of SI. 3.2. Separation of anthracene and carbazole 3.2.1. DESs for the separation of AN and CAR After the removal of PHE with xylene, the main remaining components of AN oil were AN and CAR. The DESs, as a new type of green solvents, have been widely used in the chemical industry and with good performance [17,31,32]. Ammonium-based DESs are excellent solvents to separate both basic and non-basic nitrogen compounds from fuels [15], and glycerol is a natural material and market saturated. Therefore, tetraethylammonium chloride and glycerol were used as hydrogen bond acceptor and hydrogen bond donor, respectively, to prepare DESs for the separation of AN and CAR; the separation performance of that system is summarized in Fig. 3. Clearly, the distribution coefficient and selectivity were strongly dependent on the separation temperature (Fig. 3a). For increasing temperatures, the distribution coefficient of CAR increased from 0.083 at 30 °C to 0.187 at 80 °C, while that of AN only increased slightly as compared with CAR. The viscosity and surface tension of the DESs gradually decreased with the temperature [33], making it easier for AN and CAR to partition into DESs at

high temperatures, thereby increasing the distribution coefficient. A maximum in the selectivity curve (69.0) was reached at 60 °C, due to the different rates of increase in the distribution coefficients of AN and CAR. As the DESs dose was increased, the distribution coefficient of CAR decreased within the range investigated, but a peak also appeared in the selectivity curve (Fig. 3b). The concentra- tion of CAR in the DESs decreased for increased DESs doses, which would reduce the distribution coefficient of CAR. In general, a large distribution coefficient and high selectivity favor the DESs- promoted separation of AN and CAR. Unfortunately, the high vis- cosity of the DESs could cause problems such as a low separation capacity, low operation efficiency, and equipment blockage when used directly for the separation of AN and CAR.

3.2.2. *Mixture of DESs and organic solvent for the separation of AN and CAR* Due to their high separation capacity, traditional solvents such as DMF was commonly used for the separation AN and CAR, but their low selectivity requires repeated crystallization cycles and leads to the consumption of large amounts of solvent [12]. To combine the advantages of the large separation capacity of traditional solvents with the high selectivity of DESs, these two components were mixed for the separation of AN and CAR.

Effect of organic solvent type. TEAC-glycerol DESs were selected in combination with three common organic solvents (DMF, DMA, and NMP) to investigate the separation of AN and CAR, as presented in Fig. 4, where the ordinate represents the molar amount of DESs in the mixed solvent, and the abscissa represents the distribution coefficient of CAR (Fig. 4a) and the selectivity for CAR vs. AN (Fig. 4b). Interestingly, both the distribution coefficient and the selectivity were higher for DESs-organic solvent mixtures than for pure DESs (Fig. 3). This may be due to that, as compared with pure DESs, the viscosity of the mixed system was significantly reduced, facilitating the phase transfer of CAR. When adding 50% (molar amount) of DESs, the distribution coefficient of CAR in the three mixed solvents were not very different, ranging from 0.492 to 0.531 (Fig. 4a); when the amount of DESs was reduced to 10%, the distribution coefficient of CAR in the three mixed solvents increased to 0.927 ~ 1.170, reaching a maximum value for the DESs-DMF mixture. In solvent mixtures with different amounts of DESs, the selectivity for CAR vs. AN followed the order DESs-DMF > DESs-DMA > DESs-NMP (Fig. 4b), with a maximum selectivity for CAR vs. AN (10% DESs-DMF, 231.2) more than 5 times the minimum selectivity (10% DESs-NMP, 40.0). Effect of DESS-DMF molar ratio. Since the molar ratio of DESS and DMF in the mixture had a certain influence on the separa- tion performance (as shown in Fig. 4), the influence of the DESS and DMF molar ratio on the separation of AN and CAR was investigated in more detail, and the results obtained are shown in Fig. 5, where the ordinate represents the distribution coeffi- cient of CAR or the selectivity for CAR vs. AN, and the abscissa represents the molar amount of DESs in DESs-DMF mixture. For increased molar amounts of DESs in the solvent mixture, the distribution coefficient of CAR increased from 1.20 (1% DESs) to 1.29 (5% DESs), and then decreased to 0.38 (80% DESS). Similarity, the selectivity for CAR vs. AN also increased from 89.9 to 231.2, and then decreased to 122.5 with the molar amount of DESs increased. There was a maximum in both the distribution coefficient and selectivity curves. This trend is con- sistent with results reported for the separation of tocopherol isomers using ionic liquid-organic solvent mixtures [34]. According to Yang et al. Consequently, the molar amount of DESs used in the mixed solvent system was set to 10%.

Effect of DESs type. Noted that some DESs such as choline chloride-glycerol and DMF are immiscible, the choice of hydrogen bond acceptors and hydrogen bond donors is not endless herein. ## 3.3. Separation mechanism ### 3.3.1. Structural characteristics of AN, PHE and CAR PHE and AN are isoelectronic conjugate systems, and CAR is a multi-electron conjugate system; all these molecules have seven π-orbitals. Their π-electron characteristics were investigated using of localized orbital indicator (LOL) analysis [23], presented in Fig. 7. The LOL-π (LOL purely contributed by π-orbitals) of the three six-membered rings of AN are connected, implying that delocalization of the π-electrons occurs among the three rings, and that the aromaticity of the three rings is similar. The LOL integrated π over plane (LOLIPOP) value indicating the π-stacking strength of the aromatic rings [42], are 6.22 and 5.92 for the outer rings and the central ring of AN, respectively, which shows that the tendency for π-stacking is not very different over the three rings. On the contrary, the LOL-π of the three six-membered rings of PHE is not connected, and there are three disconnections in the central ring

(shown by the black arrows in Fig. 7b). These results show that extent of π-electron conjugation (aromaticity) is higher for the outer rings than the central ring. The LOLIPOP values are 7.21 and 5.74 for the outer and central rings of PHE, respectively, meaning that the π-stacking tendency for the central ring is stronger than for the outer rings. The LOL-π of the three six-membered rings in CAR is similarly disconnected in three locations on the central five-membered ring (shown by the black arrows in Fig. 7c), which demonstrates that π-electron delocalization in CAR mainly occurs in the two outer rings. The LOLIPOP values are 7.20 and 3.70 for the outer rings and the central ring of CAR, respectively, showing again that the π-stacking tendency was higher for the central ring than for the outer rings. The π-stacking ability of the central and outer rings of CAR is significantly larger than for PHE.

The electrostatic potential (ESP), a useful tool to intuitively understand the type and intensity of electrostatic interactions between molecules [43], was analyzed for AN, PHE and CAR and the results obtained are shown in Figure S4 of SI. The order of ESP distribution ranges was CAR (-83.1 ~ 202.0 kJ/mol) > PHE (-68.7 to 92.1 kJ/mol) > AN (-66.5 to 71.5 kJ/mol). The broad ESP distribution of CAR indicates that it is more likely to interact with very polar solvents as compared with AN and PHE. The global ESP minima all appeared near the outer rings (Figure S4 of SI) for all three molecules, which contributes to the formation of π-π stacking interactions among them and with solvent molecules.

## 4. Conclusions We presented a method to separate anthracene from crude anthracene oil using mixed solvent system of DESs and organic solvents. This approach combines the advantages of the high selectivity of DESs and the large separation capacity of organic solvents. Xylene can form intermolecular interactions with phenanthrene easily, and the interactions are more complex than between xylene and anthracene or carbazole, which facilitates the removal of phenanthrene. When separating anthracene and carbazole, pure DESs achieved a high distribution coefficient and selectivity, but the separation performance was not as good as for the DESs-organic solvent mixture. Among the different conditions investigated, optimal separation performance was achieved at a molar ratio of DMF to TEAC-glycerol DESs of 9. These conditions yielded anthracene with a purity level of 97.5% in a single step, higher than achieved with an isopropanolamine-DMF mixed solvent system (92.3%). Due to the isolation of a solid product, the separation efficiency with the DESs-DMF mixed solvent is considered to be excellent. The efficient separation achieved with the DESs-DMF mixed solvent system is ascribed to N-H...Cl and C-H...π interactions

Yamaguchi (Fukuoka University, Fukuoka, Japan) www.elsevier.com/locate/molliq Effect of the addition of deep eutectic solvent to the anthracene separation <::logo: Unknown Check for updates A square button with a bookmark icon in blue, red, and yellow, above the text "Check for updates".::> Lan Yi a,b, Jie Feng a, Mario Gauthier b, Wen-Ying Li a,* a State Key Laboratory of Clean and Efficient Coal Utilization, Taiyuan University of Technology, Taiyuan 030024, PR China b School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Wuhan University of Science and Technology, Wuhan 430081, PR China ## ARTICLE INFO --- *Article history:* Received 8 May 2021 Revised 10 June 2021 Accepted 16 June 2021 Available online 18 June 2021 --- *Keywords:* Anthracene Deep eutectic solvents Separation mechanism Intermolecular interaction ABSTRACT Anthracene (AN) is an important fine chemical feedstock, mainly derived from the anthracene oil fraction of high-temperature coal tar. The traditional solvent crystallization method used to obtain anthracene involves large amounts of solvents. A method with a high separation capacity and a high selectivity needs to be developed urgently. To this end, the composition of crude AN oil and the solubility of its main components in xylene were determined, and phenanthrene in crude AN oil was extracted with xylene. Pure deep eutectic solvents (DESs) and DESs–organic solvent mixture were then applied to separate anthracene and carbazole, respectively. Based on the distribution coefficient, selectivity, and purity of the AN product, the influence of organic solvent type, the molar ratio of DESs to organic solvent, and DESs type on the separation efficiency were investigated. Finally, the separation mechanism was investigated with density functional theory calculations and UV-visible spectroscopy. The results show that the phenanthrene content decreased from 25.5% to 2.6% and most of other condensed aromatics in crude AN were removed after washing twice with xylene. DESs–organic solvent mixtures had better performance than pure DESs for the separation of anthracene and carbazole, and under optimal condition, the 97.5% purity of AN is acquired in a single separation step with a tetraethyl ammonium chloride–glycerol DESs–DMF mixture. The more complicated interactions between phenanthrene and xylene than between anthracene / carbazole and xylene favored the removal of phenanthrene. The hydrogen bond with the minimum bond energy (–17.6 kJ/mol) between DESs and carbazole is also stronger than that with the maximum bond energy (–16.8 kJ/mol) between DESs and anthracene. Adding DESs to organic solvent can enhance the interactions between carbazole and the solvent, but had no significantly influence on interactions between anthracene and the solvent, thereby facilitating the separation of anthracene and carbazole. © 2021 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. ## 1. Introduction Crude anthracene oil, a fraction distilled from high-temperature coal tar, is a mixture consisting of condensed aromatic compounds with 2–5 aromatic rings [1]. Among the condensed aromatics are anthracene (AN), carbazole (CAR), and phenanthrene (PHE), which account for more than 1 wt% of high-temperature coal tar. AN, one of the most valuable components in coal tar, is an irreplaceable raw material in the manufacture of dyes, bactericides, pesticides, light-emitting diodes, and so on [2,3]. For the production of fine chemicals, AN with a purity higher than 98% is essential. The remaining 2% impurities, which are difficult to remove, include CAR [4]. Much effort is need to improve the purity of AN while refining crude AN * Corresponding author. E-mail address: ying@tyut.edu.cn (W.-Y. Li). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molliq.2021.116762 0167-7322/© 2021 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. oil, as the separation and purification of AN is usually accompanied by the simultaneous removal of CAR. Commonly used methods to isolate AN include distillation, supercritical fluid extraction, zone melting, emulsion membrane separation, and solvent crystallization [5-7] and each method has its own advantages and disadvantages [7,8]. For example, distillation has the advantage of continuous operation and the disadvantage of high energy consumption; supercritical fluids extraction has a high extraction efficiency for aromatics, but require harsh operating conditions; the zone melting technique is complex to operate, and the emulsion membrane separation method is unstable. Ionic liquids (ILs), known as green solvents, are also being investigated in the refining of crude AN oil, and it was shown that 66.6% recovery and 90.2% purity of CAR separated from anthracene oil could be achieved [9]. However, as a new separation technology, the use of ILs in crude AN oil refining still faces difficulties in implementation [10], requiring further investigations and studies. L. Yi, J. Feng, M. Unfortunately, repeated crystallization processes consume large amounts of solvent. Due to the similarity in structure of AN and CAR, solvent extraction processes cannot guarantee large distribution coefficients and high selectivity. In recent studies, the AN purity attained by solvent extraction typically reached 90–95% [11], with a maximum purity of about 97% [12]. Due to the limitations of these separation techniques, a new method using a third component in traditional organic solvents was proposed and yielded promising results. For instance, adding supercritical CO2 to acetone promoted the separation of AN and PHE [13]; dissolving an amide/amine combination in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) improved the solubility of PHE in that solvent [11]. In research by Ye et al. [7,14], it was shown that the addition of isopropanolamine, urea, and H2O to DMF improved the separation selectivity for AN and CAR significantly. The enhanced separation efficiency was ascribed to the electron-rich atoms or groups in the additives, introducing intermolecular interactions such as hydrogen bonds with the –NH group of CAR [14]. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), similar to ILs, have a broad liquid temperature range, a low vapor pressure, a high chemical stability, and were used for the removal of CAR from fuels [15]. Due to the formation of hydrogen bond between the DESs and CAR, efficient fuel denitrogenation was achieved. DESs include both hydrogen bond donors and hydrogen bond acceptors, facilitating the formation of intermolecular interactions with target components. Correspondingly, the performance of DESs was excellent in the extraction and isolation of many components including phenolic compounds [16,17], nitrogen/sulfur- containing compounds [18], benzene derivatives [19], and metals [20]. The application of DESs as solvents or additives to refine crude AN oil has not been reported, however. In this study, the solubility of AN, PHE, and CAR in xylene were determined and PHE was first extracted from crude AN oil with xylene. DESs were then used as separation agents or additives in organic solvent for the separation of AN and CAR. The separation efficiency of DESs, either pure or mixed with solvents was investi- gated, as well as the separation mechanism involved. ## 2. Experimental and calculation section ### 2.1. Chemical reagents Analytical pure Anthracene (AN), carbazole (CAR), and phenanthrene (PHE) were purchased from Macleans Reagent Co., Ltd. Glycerol (99 wt%), levulinic acid (99 wt%), malonic acid (99.5 wt%), 9-fluorenone (98 wt%), Tetraethyl ammonium chloride (TEAC, 98 wt%), and tetrapropylammonium chloride (TPAC, 98 wt%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co. Analytical pure N,N-dimethyl formamide (DMF), N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP), N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMA), hexane, and xylene were purchased from Tianjin Kemiou Chemical Co. Acetonitrile (HPLC pure) was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co. Crude anthracene oil was provided by one steel factory, Wuhan, China. The composition was detected by GC-MS (7890B GC system, 5977A MSD; Agilent Technology). ## 2.2. Preparation of DESs and AN-CAR mixture The preparation procedure for TEAC–glycerol DESs was provided herein as an example, where TEAC and glycerol were selected as the HBA and HBD, respectively. In a typical process, TEAC and glycerol were mixed at equimolar ratio in a capped conical flask and agitated with magnetic stirring at 80 °C until the liquid became homogeneous. Other DESs were prepared in a similar way. AN-CAR mixture was prepared by dissolving AN and CAR in hot benzene and evaporating benzene after AN and CAR were completely dissolved. 2.3. Separation experiments Separation of AN and CAR. The AN–CAR mixture was added to the prepared DESs and stirred magnetically for 30 min at the set temperature. Filtered them to obtain cake and filtrate at room temperature. A small amount of cake and filtrate were respectively collected and analyzed by the UV–visible spectrophotometer. The 2 L. Yi, J. Separation of crude anthracene oil. The crude anthracene oil mainly contains 34.1 wt% AN, 25.5 wt% PHE, and 16.4 wt% CAR. The separation experiment on crude anthracene oil was conducted as follows: 100 g crude anthracene oil and 60 ml xylene were mixed in a 500 ml flask equipped with a reflux condenser pipe and stirred magnetically for 30 min at 120 °C in an oil bath. After the crude anthracene oil was completely dissolved in xylene, this mixture was filtered at 30 °C to obtain the first filter cake. Subse- quently, the first filter cake was mixed with xylene at the liquid/- solid ratio of 1.5:1 and the conditions of stirring and filtering were the same as the above. And the second filter cake rich in AN and CAR was obtained and dried at 40 °C for 12 h. The dried second fil- ter cake was mixed with DESS-DMF solvent, magnetically stirred at a set temperature for 30 min, and filtered at room temperature to get AN product. Take a small amount of product for GC detection to determine the purity. ## 2.4. Analytical methods The content of AN and CAR in cake and filtrate for measuring distribution coefficient was analyzed by UV-visible spectrophotometer (CARY 300). The UV-vis absorption peaks of CAR and AN at 292 nm and 378 nm had no overlap and no mutual interference (Figure S1 of supporting information) and they were selected as the characteristic absorption wavelengths of CAR and AN respectively for quantitative calculation. UV-visible spectral experiments were also carried out to verify the interactions between solvent and AN or CAR. The sample scan range was 220 to 420 nm. The compositions of crude AN oil and AN product were detected by GC–MS (7890B GC system, 5977A MSD; Agilent Technology), equipped with a HP-5 capillary column (30 m × 0.32 mm × 0.25 µm) and a flame ionization detector (FID). The chromatographic detection temperature conditions were 280 °C for the over and injector, and 300 °C for the detector. The MS detection conditions were a temperature of 250 °C for the detector, 70 eV emission volt- age, and mass range of 33–400 Da. 2.5. More than five initial geometries for compound or conformation were optimized under no symmetry restrictions at the M06-2X/6-31 + G(d,p) level. The single-point energy was computed at the M06-2X/6-311++G (d,p) level and the counterpoise procedure [22] was considered to correct the basis set superposition error (BSSE). Electrostatic potential (ESP) [24] was used to analyze nucleophilic and elec- trophilic sites of AN, PHE and CAR. Reduced density gradient (RDG) [25] was used to analyze the weak interaction between xylene and AN or PHE or CAR. Independent gradient model (IGM) [26] was used to visually study the interactions between DESS and AN, CAR, or DMF. Atoms in molecules (AIM) population [27] was used to identify the hydrogen bond and van der Waals (vdW) interaction. The wave function was analyzed using the pro- gram Multiwfn 3.6 [28] and all the isosurfaces were described using VMD 1.9.2 [29]. ## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Removal of PHE from crude AN oil The composition of crude AN oil is shown in Fig. 1. PHE (25.5%), AN (34.1%), and CAR (16.4%) were the main components of crude AN oil, with small amounts of fluorene, dibenzofuran, dibenzothio-phene and other fused ring aromatic compounds. Note that 9-fluorenone was used as internal standard for the analysis. Xylene, an aromatic solvent, was used to extract PHE from the crude AN oil. Before the separation, the solubility of AN, PHE, and CAR in xylene and the solubility selectivity for PHE vs. CAR (AN) were determined as described in the Supporting Information (SI); the result obtained summarized in Fig. 2. It can be seen that at 30 °C, the solubility of PHE in xylene was nearly 38 times higher than CAR and 18 times higher than AN, indicating that xylene is capable of removing PHE from crude AN oil. Similarly to PHE, xylene is a weakly polar molecule, so it can dissolve a certain amount of PHE in agreement with the "like dissolves like" rule. The dipole moments calculated (at m062x/def2-TZVPD level) for AN, CAR, PHE and xylene were 0, 1.66, 0.01, and 0.42 D, respectively. AN is a non-polar molecule due to its completely symmetrical structure, while CAR is strongly polar due to its -NH bond. Clearly, the inter-actions between xylene and AN or CAR are insufficient to compete with the interactions between AN molecules or CAR molecules, resulting in low solubility of AN and CAR in xylene. Separation of anthracene and carbazole 3.2.1. DESs for the separation of AN and CAR After the removal of PHE with xylene, the main remaining components of AN oil were AN and CAR. The DESs, as a new type of green solvents, have been widely used in the chemical industry and with good performance [17,31,32]. Ammonium-based DESs are excellent solvents to separate both basic and non-basic nitrogen compounds from fuels [15], and glycerol is a natural material and market saturated. Therefore, tetraethylammonium chloride and glycerol were used as hydrogen bond acceptor and hydrogen bond donor, respectively, to prepare DESs for the separation of AN and CAR; the separation performance of that system is summarized in Fig. 3. Clearly, the distribution coefficient and selectivity were strongly dependent on the separation temperature (Fig. 3a). For increasing temperatures, the distribution coefficient of CAR increased from 0.083 at 30 °C to 0.187 at 80 °C, while that of AN only increased slightly as compared with CAR. The viscosity and surface tension of the DESs gradually decreased with the temperature [33], making it easier for AN and CAR to partition into DESs at high temperatures, thereby increasing the distribution coefficient. A maximum in the selectivity curve (69.0) was reached at 60 °C, due to the different rates of increase in the distribution coefficients of AN and CAR. As the DESs dose was increased, the distribution coefficient of CAR decreased within the range investigated, but a peak also appeared in the selectivity curve (Fig. 3b). The concentra- tion of CAR in the DESs decreased for increased DESs doses, which would reduce the distribution coefficient of CAR. Structural characteristics of AN, PHE and CAR PHE and AN are isoelectronic conjugate systems, and CAR is a multi-electron conjugate system; all these molecules have seven π-orbitals. Their π-electron characteristics were investigated using of localized orbital indicator (LOL) analysis [23], presented in Fig. 7. The LOL-π (LOL purely contributed by π-orbitals) of the three six-membered rings of AN are connected, implying that delocalization of the π-electrons occurs among the three rings, and that the aromaticity of the three rings is similar. The LOL integrated π over plane (LOLIPOP) value indicating the π-stacking strength of the aromatic rings [42], are 6.22 and 5.92 for the outer rings and the central ring of AN, respectively, which shows that the tendency for π-stacking is not very different over the three rings. On the contrary, the LOL-π of the three six-membered rings of PHE is not connected, and there are three disconnections in the central ring (shown by the black arrows in Fig. 7b). These results show that extent of π-electron conjugation (aromaticity) is higher for the outer rings than the central ring. The LOLIPOP values are 7.21 and 5.74 for the outer and central rings of PHE, respectively, meaning that the π-stacking tendency for the central ring is stronger than for the outer rings. The LOL-π of the three six-membered rings in CAR is similarly disconnected in three locations on the central five-membered ring (shown by the black arrows in Fig. 7c), which demonstrates that π-electron delocalization in CAR mainly occurs in the two outer rings. The LOLIPOP values are 7.20 and 3.70 for the outer rings and the central ring of CAR, respectively, showing again that the π-stacking tendency was higher for the central ring than for the outer rings. The π-stacking ability of the central and outer rings of CAR is significantly larger than for PHE. The electrostatic potential (ESP), a useful tool to intuitively understand the type and intensity of electrostatic interactions between molecules [43], was analyzed for AN, PHE and CAR and the results obtained are shown in Figure S4 of SI. The order of ESP distribution ranges was CAR (-83.1 ~ 202.0 kJ/mol) > PHE (-68.7 to 92.1 kJ/mol) > AN (-66.5 to 71.5 kJ/mol). The broad ESP distribution of CAR indicates that it is more likely to interact with very polar solvents as compared with AN and PHE. The global ESP minima all appeared near the outer rings (Figure S4 of SI) for all three molecules, which contributes to the formation of π-π stacking interactions among them and with solvent molecules. 3.3.2. Conclusions We presented a method to separate anthracene from crude anthracene oil using mixed solvent system of DESs and organic solvents. This approach combines the advantages of the high selectivity of DESs and the large separation capacity of organic solvents. Xylene can form intermolecular interactions with phenanthrene easily, and the interactions are more complex than between xylene and anthracene or carbazole, which facilitates the removal of phenanthrene. When separating anthracene and carbazole, pure DESs achieved a high distribution coefficient and selectivity, but the separation performance was not as good as for the DESs-organic solvent mixture. Among the different conditions investigated, optimal separation performance was achieved at a molar ratio of DMF to TEAC-glycerol DESs of 9. These conditions yielded anthracene with a purity level of 97.5% in a single step, higher than achieved with an isopropanolamine-DMF mixed solvent system (92.3%). Due to the isolation of a solid product, the separation efficiency with the DESs-DMF mixed solvent is considered to be excellent. In recent studies, the AN purity attained by solvent extraction typically reached 90–95% [11], with a maximum purity of about 97% [12]. Due to the limitations of these separation techniques, a new method using a third component in traditional organic solvents was proposed and yielded promising results. For instance, adding supercritical CO2 to acetone promoted the separation of AN and PHE [13]; dissolving an amide/amine combination in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) improved the solubility of PHE in that solvent [11]. In research by Ye et al. [7,14], it was shown that the addition of isopropanolamine, urea, and H2O to DMF improved the separation selectivity for AN and CAR significantly. The enhanced separation efficiency was ascribed to the electron-rich atoms or groups in the additives, introducing intermolecular interactions such as hydrogen bonds with the –NH group of CAR [14]. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), similar to ILs, have a broad liquid temperature range, a low vapor pressure, a high chemical stability, and were used for the removal of CAR from fuels [15]. Due to the formation of hydrogen bond between the DESs and CAR, efficient fuel denitrogenation was achieved. DESs include both hydrogen bond donors and hydrogen bond acceptors, facilitating the formation of intermolecular interactions with target components. Correspondingly, the performance of DESs was excellent in the extraction and isolation of many components including phenolic compounds [16,17], nitrogen/sulfur- containing compounds [18], benzene derivatives [19], and metals [20]. The application of DESs as solvents or additives to refine crude AN oil has not been reported, however. DESs were then used as separation agents or additives in organic solvent for the separation of AN and CAR. Structural characteristics of AN, PHE and CAR PHE and AN are isoelectronic conjugate systems, and CAR is a multi-electron conjugate system; all these molecules have seven π-orbitals. Their π-electron characteristics were investigated using of localized orbital indicator (LOL) analysis [23], presented in Fig. 7. The LOL-π (LOL purely contributed by π-orbitals) of the three six-membered rings of AN are connected, implying that delocalization of the π-electrons occurs among the three rings, and that the aromaticity of the three rings is similar. The LOL integrated π over plane (LOLIPOP) value indicating the π-stacking strength of the aromatic rings [42], are 6.22 and 5.92 for the outer rings and the central ring of AN, respectively, which shows that the tendency for π-stacking is not very different over the three rings. On the contrary, the LOL-π of the three six-membered rings of PHE is not connected, and there are three disconnections in the central ring (shown by the black arrows in Fig. 7b). These results show that extent of π-electron conjugation (aromaticity) is higher for the outer rings than the central ring. The LOLIPOP values are 7.21 and 5.74 for the outer and central rings of PHE, respectively, meaning that the π-stacking tendency for the central ring is stronger than for the outer rings. The LOL-π of the three six-membered rings in CAR is similarly disconnected in three locations on the central five-membered ring (shown by the black arrows in Fig. 7c), which demonstrates that π-electron delocalization in CAR mainly occurs in the two outer rings. The LOLIPOP values are 7.20 and 3.70 for the outer rings and the central ring of CAR, respectively, showing again that the π-stacking tendency was higher for the central ring than for the outer rings. The π-stacking ability of the central and outer rings of CAR is significantly larger than for PHE. The electrostatic potential (ESP), a useful tool to intuitively understand the type and intensity of electrostatic interactions between molecules [43], was analyzed for AN, PHE and CAR and the results obtained are shown in Figure S4 of SI. The order of ESP distribution ranges was CAR (-83.1 ~ 202.0 kJ/mol) > PHE (-68.7 to 92.1 kJ/mol) > AN (-66.5 to 71.5 kJ/mol). The broad ESP distribution of CAR indicates that it is more likely to interact with very polar solvents as compared with AN and PHE. The global ESP minima all appeared near the outer rings (Figure S4 of SI) for all three molecules, which contributes to the formation of π-π stacking interactions among them and with solvent molecules. 3.3.2. Conclusions We presented a method to separate anthracene from crude anthracene oil using mixed solvent system of DESs and organic solvents. This approach combines the advantages of the high selectivity of DESs and the large separation capacity of organic solvents. Xylene can form intermolecular interactions with phenanthrene easily, and the interactions are more complex than between xylene and anthracene or carbazole, which facilitates the removal of phenanthrene. When separating anthracene and carbazole, pure DESs achieved a high distribution coefficient and selectivity, but the separation performance was not as good as for the DESs-organic solvent mixture. Among the different conditions investigated, optimal separation performance was achieved at a molar ratio of DMF to TEAC-glycerol DESs of 9. These conditions yielded anthracene with a purity level of 97.5% in a single step, higher than achieved with an isopropanolamine-DMF mixed solvent system (92.3%). Due to the isolation of a solid product, the separation efficiency with the DESs-DMF mixed solvent is considered to be excellent.
